prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "ASTRAZENECA PLC" (ticker AZN), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "AZN", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: AstraZeneca PLC
markets: Oncology (lung, breast, blood and other cancers)

mission.statement: We push the boundaries of science to deliver life-changing medicines.
mission.source: AstraZeneca website, Our company (astrazeneca.com/our-company), stated as its purpose
mission.plain: AstraZeneca wants to use cutting-edge science to make medicines that change patients' lives.

about.plain: AstraZeneca is a big British-Swedish company that invents and makes medicines. Its biggest area is cancer drugs, like pills and infusions that help people with lung or breast cancer live longer. It also makes medicines for the heart, kidneys, lungs and very rare diseases. It spends billions of dollars a year on research to find new medicines.
about.customers: Hospitals, pharmacies, governments and health insurers in over 100 countries buy its medicines, which doctors prescribe to patients.
about.everyday: Many people remember AstraZeneca for the COVID-19 vaccine it developed with Oxford University, and millions take its diabetes and heart drug Farxiga or use its Symbicort and Breztri inhalers.

money.plain: cancer drugs such as Tagrisso, Imfinzi, Enhertu, Calquence and Lynparza
drugs like Farxiga for diabetes, heart failure and kidney disease
very expensive drugs like Ultomiris and Soliris for rare blood and nerve diseases
asthma and COPD inhalers and injections such as Breztri, Fasenra and Tezspire
a new pill for hard-to-control high blood pressure, launched in the US in Q2 2026
experimental pills and injections for obesity, such as the oral GLP-1 drug AZD5004

result.summary: AstraZeneca has a strong moat built on patents, a deep and productive pipeline (43 approvals in major regions in the twelve months to February 2026 and more than 100 Phase 3 trials) and global commercial scale, especially in oncology and in China. The advantage is real but must be constantly renewed, because each drug loses protection: Farxiga generics hit the US in 2026, and pricing pressure from US policy and China's volume-based procurement is rising.

pricingPower.evidence: Patent-protected cancer drugs keep growing fast at premium prices (Imfinzi +31% and Enhertu +36% in H1 2026), but AstraZeneca agreed in October 2025 to offer US cash-pay patients up to 80% off list prices via TrumpRx, Farxiga faces US generics (US Farxiga sales down 17% in H1 2026) and Medicare price negotiation, and China's volume-based procurement cuts prices on older drugs.

moats.evidence: Patents and regulatory exclusivity protect blockbusters such as Tagrisso ($7,254M FY2025 sales), Imfinzi ($6,063M) and Ultomiris ($4,718M), and physicians trust the brand as a leader in lung cancer.

Patients doing well on a cancer or rare-disease therapy are rarely switched, and Ultomiris has retained Soliris patients, but payers can force switches when generics or cheaper rivals arrive, as with Farxiga in 2026.
Medicines have little network effect, although its large clinical-trial networks and physician relationships make it easier to recruit patients for new studies.
With $58,739M of FY2025 revenue and $14,232M of R&D spending, AstraZeneca can fund more than 100 Phase 3 trials and global launches that smaller rivals cannot afford.
Rare-disease markets such as PNH and generalised myasthenia gravis are small enough that only one or two companies can profitably serve them, which supports Alexion's position.

Its early, large-scale bet on China and emerging markets ($6,654M of China revenue in FY2025) gave it a position that Western peers were slow to copy, but it is not a business model incumbents cannot follow.

Under Pascal Soriot, R&D productivity rose sharply (16 positive Phase 3 readouts and 43 approvals in the year to February 2026), and its antibody-drug conjugate know-how with Daiichi Sankyo (Enhertu, Datroway) is hard to replicate.
Exclusive partnerships and acquisitions such as Alexion (2021) and the Daiichi Sankyo ADC alliance give it unique assets, but rivals can buy or license competing science.

customers.evidence: Doctors keep prescribing its leading drugs: Tagrisso is standard first-line therapy for EGFR-mutated lung cancer and Ultomiris product revenue grew 16% in H1 2026, though patients and payers are price-sensitive and loyalty breaks when generics arrive.

talent.evidence: AstraZeneca employs about 96,100 people (2025 annual report) and has repeatedly ranked near the top of Science magazine's Top Employers survey of biopharma companies, helped by its science-led reputation and its Cambridge, Gothenburg and Gaithersburg R&D hubs.

product.evidence: Several medicines are best in class or standard of care, including Tagrisso in EGFR lung cancer, Enhertu in HER2 breast cancer and Ultomiris in PNH, backed by 30 approvals in major regions in the first half of 2026.

marketShare.measure: revenue share (AstraZeneca oncology revenue was $25,619M in FY2025; market totals and peer shares not verified)

marketShare.market: SGLT2 inhibitors (diabetes, heart failure, kidney disease)
marketShare.measure: revenue share (Farxiga vs Jardiance; exact shares not verified)

marketShare.market: Complement inhibitors for rare diseases (PNH, aHUS, gMG)
marketShare.measure: revenue share (Ultomiris and Soliris lead; exact shares not verified)

threats: Loss of exclusivity: multiple US generics of Farxiga (FY2025 sales $8,405M) launched in Q2 2026, and Tagrisso, Lynparza and Soliris face patent expiries or biosimilars over the coming years
US drug-pricing policy: Medicare price negotiation under the Inflation Reduction Act and the October 2025 US government agreement (TrumpRx, up to 80% off list prices for cash-pay patients)
China risk: volume-based procurement price cuts and the 2024 detention of its China president Leon Wang amid local investigations, in a market worth $6,654M of FY2025 revenue
Competition in immuno-oncology and lung cancer from Merck's Keytruda and Johnson & Johnson's Rybrevant, and in BTK inhibitors from BeOne's Brukinsa
Clinical trial failures in key late-stage programmes such as Datroway, baxdrostat and obesity drugs
Rising net debt ($26,912M at June 30, 2026) and heavy spending, including the $50 billion US manufacturing and R&D commitment over five years
CEO succession risk after more than a decade under Pascal Soriot

ceo.name: Pascal Soriot
ceo.background: French-born veterinarian (École Nationale Vétérinaire d'Alfort) with an MBA from HEC Paris; previously COO of Roche's pharmaceuticals division and CEO of Genentech; knighted in 2022

c1.evidence: AstraZeneca leads important fast-growing fields such as antibody-drug conjugates (Enhertu +36% in H1 2026) and EGFR lung cancer, but pharmaceuticals as a whole is a mature industry.

c2.evidence: Doctors choose its drugs for clinical data that show longer survival (Tagrisso, Imfinzi, Enhertu), and patents protect that for years, but each advantage expires, as Farxiga's 2026 US generics show.

c3.evidence: The name became widely known through the Oxford COVID-19 vaccine, but it is not the default leader of pharma the way Google is in search; Merck, Roche and Eli Lilly are equally prominent.

c4.evidence: Its purpose 'We push the boundaries of science to deliver life-changing medicines' and its ambition to 'eliminate cancer as a cause of death' are emphasised consistently, and its at-cost COVID-19 vaccine supply in 2020-2021 showed purpose beyond profit.

c6.evidence: “COVID vaccine, cancer drugs, British pharma giant”: the impression is mostly positive for its science and pandemic role, though tempered by the vaccine's rare blood-clot side effects and general distrust of drug pricing.

c7.evidence: Its markets (cancer, cardiometabolic, respiratory and rare diseases) are large and growing with ageing populations, and it targets $80 billion of revenue in 2030 versus $58,739M in FY2025.

c8.evidence: It is expanding into obesity (oral GLP-1 AZD5004), hypertension (Baxfendy launched in the US in Q2 2026), cell therapy and radioconjugates, and committed $50 billion to US manufacturing and R&D over five years.

m1.evidence: Soriot set bold, specific goals and largely met them, from the 2014 defence against Pfizer's takeover bid to the 2030 ambition of 20 new medicines and $80 billion of revenue.

m2.evidence: Not a founder, but in 14 years as CEO since 2012 Soriot has rebuilt the company around long-term R&D, raising R&D spending to $14,232M in FY2025.

m4.evidence: There is little independent evidence about Soriot's leadership style toward employees, though he champions a patient-first, science-led culture.

m5.evidence: Soriot deliberately rebuilt a science-led R&D culture that turned a weak pipeline into one with 43 approvals in major regions in the year to February 2026 and more than 100 Phase 3 studies.

m6.evidence: Soriot is a trained veterinarian with deep scientific and commercial knowledge rather than an engineer, and he is closely involved in pipeline and deal decisions.

m7.evidence: He led the decision to supply the Oxford COVID-19 vaccine at no profit during the pandemic and was knighted in 2022 for services to UK life sciences and the COVID-19 response.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Pascal Soriot at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar university could be confirmed.

m8b.evidence: Soriot is respected and outspoken on UK life-sciences policy, but he does not have a celebrity persona like Elon Musk or Alex Karp.

m9.evidence: Under Soriot, Total Revenue more than doubled from $26,617M in FY2020 to $58,739M in FY2025 and reported operating profit rose from $1,056M in FY2021 to $13,743M in FY2025.

m10.evidence: AstraZeneca is not known for frugality; Soriot is among the highest-paid FTSE 100 CEOs and the company spends heavily on R&D and acquisitions.

c10.evidence: Its medicines treat millions of patients worldwide, and its COVID-19 vaccine (Vaxzevria) supplied around three billion doses, mostly at no profit, during the pandemic.

p2.evidence: Discovering, testing and winning approval for new medicines takes over a decade and billions of dollars, and AstraZeneca spent $14,232M on R&D in FY2025 to do it.

f1.evidence: Total Revenue rose every year from $26,617M in FY2020 to $37,417M, $44,351M, $45,811M, $54,073M and $58,739M in FY2025.

f2.evidence: Reported gross margin rose from 66.0% in FY2021 to 82% in FY2025 and operating margin from 2.8% to 23.4%, though FY2021 was depressed by Alexion acquisition accounting.

f3.evidence: Net debt was $26,912M at June 30, 2026 against cash of $4,893M, about 1.8 times FY2025 operating cash flow of $14,575M, with positive shareholders' equity; manageable but not low.

f4.evidence: Reported operating profit rose each year from $1,056M in FY2021 to $13,743M in FY2025, and operating cash flow from $9,808M in FY2022 to $14,575M in FY2025.

v1.evidence: Several drugs are clearly best in their niche (Tagrisso is first-line standard for EGFR lung cancer because it extends survival), but across its portfolio rivals such as Keytruda and Jardiance are as good or better.

v2.evidence: AstraZeneca has repeatedly ranked near the top of Science magazine's Top Employers survey for biopharma, but it is not usually listed among the very best workplaces across all industries.

c5.evidence: If AstraZeneca disappeared, patients with lung and breast cancer, rare diseases such as PNH and chronic heart, kidney and lung conditions would lose medicines that extend and improve their lives, and many have no equivalent alternative.
